# Te Tiriti Entrenchment Policy 2026

Source: [https://img.scoop.co.nz/media/pdfs/2609/TIRITI_ENTRENCHMENT_POLICY.pdf](https://img.scoop.co.nz/media/pdfs/2609/TIRITI_ENTRENCHMENT_POLICY.pdf). Attached by Te Pāti Māori to its 1 Sep 2026 press release (Scoop PA2609/S00008).

> Extraction notes: text is reproduced in the PDF's content-stream order, page by page. Only whitespace and glyph markup were normalised (bullet glyphs shown as •, decorative icons removed). Designed layouts mean page headers, side labels and table cells can appear out of visual order; consult the PDF for layout. No words were added, removed or reworded.

## Full text

### Page 1

```text
TE TIRITI ENTRENCHMENT POLICY 2026 | POLICY
TE PĀTI MĀORI • TE TIRITI ENTRENCHMENT POLICY 2026
POLICY
Te Tiriti Entrenchment Policy
Executive Summary
Te Tiriti o Waitangi is the constitutional foundation of Aotearoa. It is not a creation of Parliament, and
its authority does not depend on Parliament's permission.
Successive governments have nevertheless treated Crown obligations under Te Tiriti as politically
discretionary, able to be weakened, removed or ignored by the Government of the day.
Te Pāti Māori will change that by creating durable and enforceable minimum obligations on the
Crown, strengthening remedies when breaches occur, and resourcing Māori-led constitutional
transformation.
The purpose is to entrench the Crown's conduct, not to entrench a Crown version of Te Tiriti.
The legislation will not constitute, define, replace, limit or domesticate Te Tiriti. It will bind Ministers,
departments and Crown agencies to obligations that arise from Te Tiriti itself.
Context
He Whakaputanga o te Rangatiratanga o Nu Tireni, signed in 1835, affirmed the mana and
rangatiratanga of the rangatira and hapū of Aotearoa before Te Tiriti o Waitangi was signed. It
declared that sovereign authority resided with the rangatira and hapū and could not simply be
assumed by another authority.
Te Tiriti o Waitangi followed in 1840. It did not extinguish that authority. Te Tiriti established a
relationship between continuing Māori authority and the authority exercised by the Crown.
Te Tiriti o Waitangi precedes New Zealand's parliamentary system. It established an enduring
relationship between Māori authority and Crown authority. As a consequence, legislation cannot be
the source of Te Tiriti o Waitangi’s mana.
The problem is that Crown institutions have too often acted as though the Crown can decide when,
how and to what extent its Te Tiriti obligations apply.
Māori should not continually have to take the Crown to court to make it honour Te Tiriti. Nor should
Te Tiriti protections depend on the political preferences of the Government of the day.
Mātike Mai Aotearoa has already undertaken foundational Māori-led constitutional work. The
Waitangi Tribunal has established an extensive record of Crown breaches. Aotearoa has endorsed
the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. What is missing is enforceable
accountability and the resources to advance the next stage.
```

### Page 2

```text
TE TIRITI ENTRENCHMENT POLICY 2026 | POLICY
TE PĀTI MĀORI • TE TIRITI ENTRENCHMENT POLICY 2026
Our Position
• We acknowledge He Whakaputanga o te Rangatiratanga o Nu Tireni as the foundational
assertion of the mana and rangatiratanga of Māori and the constitutional authority of rangatira
and hapū.
• Te Tiriti did not create Māori authority. It recognised a relationship with authority that already
existed.
• Te Tiriti o Waitangi has authority in its own right. Parliament does not give Te Tiriti its mana.
• Tino rangatiratanga is an authority, not an advisory interest.
• Legislation should bind Crown conduct to Te Tiriti, not bring Te Tiriti under Parliamentary
control.
• Te Tiriti o Waitangi in te reo Māori will be the primary reference point for Crown obligations.
• The Crown must be legally accountable when it breaches its Te Tiriti obligations.
• Constitutional transformation must be led by iwi, hapū and Māori, not imposed by political
parties.
• Te Pāti Māori’s role is a mahi function, not a mana function. Our role is to resource the
people to determine the constitutional future for themselves.
Te Pāti Māori will:
1. Establish a Mātike Mai Fund
Establish a dedicated Mātike Mai Fund of $220 million over four years to independently resource the
next stage of constitutional transformation.
The Fund will:
1. establish and resource an independent Mātike Mai secretariat;
2. fund iwi, hapū and Māori-led constitutional kōrero across every rohe;
3. resource the further independent working group envisaged by Mātike Mai;
4. support nationwide constitutional engagement, including rangatahi participation;
5. convene a Māori Constitutional Convention and begin formal dialogue with tangata Tiriti,
local government and the Crown; and
6. progress toward a national Tiriti Convention.
Te Pāti Māori will establish 2040 as the target for constitutional transformation in Aotearoa.
2. Implement the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples
Within the first 100 days, Te Pāti Māori will restore and resource development of a national action
plan to implement the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples.
Aotearoa has already endorsed UNDRIP. What is missing is a domestic implementation framework.
The plan will identify the legislative, policy and institutional changes required to give practical effect
to Indigenous rights, with meaningful and independent Māori participation.
```

### Page 3

```text
TE TIRITI ENTRENCHMENT POLICY 2026 | POLICY
TE PĀTI MĀORI • TE TIRITI ENTRENCHMENT POLICY 2026
UNDRIP will complement, not replace, Te Tiriti.
3. Establish an Independent Te Tiriti Commission
Establish an independent Te Tiriti Commission as an Officer of Parliament, with expertise in Te Tiriti,
tikanga Māori, constitutional law and Māori-Crown relations.
The Commission will not define Te Tiriti or become the source of its meaning. Its role is to
independently assess and enforce the Crown's minimum statutory obligations arising from Te Tiriti.
Its governance and appointment arrangements will include meaningful Māori participation and
protect the Commission from control by the Government of the day.
The Commission will operate independently of the Government of the day and will have statutory
powers to:
1. investigate Crown decisions, policy and Executive action for Te Tiriti compliance;
2. require information and evidence from Ministers, departments and Crown agencies;
3. report directly to Parliament on breaches and systemic failures;
4. require remedial action where Crown processes fail to meet Te Tiriti obligations;
5. stop or suspend Executive decisions where a serious breach is found; and
6. create Te Tiriti Compliance Orders
Where the Commission finds that an Executive decision seriously breaches statutory Te Tiriti
obligations, it may issue a Te Tiriti Compliance Order stopping or suspending that decision.
If the Crown disagrees, it must apply to the High Court to have the order overturned. Until the Court
determines otherwise, the order remains in force.
This reverses the burden of accountability: where a serious breach is found, the Crown must justify
why it should be permitted to proceed.
The Commission will not invalidate an Act of Parliament. It may, however, assess proposed
legislation and report directly to Parliament where a Bill is inconsistent with Te Tiriti.
5. Make Waitangi Tribunal recommendations binding
Amend the Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975 so that Waitangi Tribunal recommendations are binding on
the Crown, with clear implementation timeframes, reporting requirements and judicial enforcement
where necessary.
The two institutions will have complementary roles:
• The Waitangi Tribunal will investigate breaches and provide binding remedies.
• The Te Tiriti Commission will scrutinise Executive action and seek to prevent serious
breaches before they occur.
Together, they make the Crown accountable for remedying breaches and for preventing new ones.
```

### Page 4

```text
TE TIRITI ENTRENCHMENT POLICY 2026 | POLICY
TE PĀTI MĀORI • TE TIRITI ENTRENCHMENT POLICY 2026
Our Commitment
Te Pāti Māori will move Crown responsibility under Te Tiriti from political discretion to enforceable
legal obligation.
We will not ask Parliament to give Te Tiriti its authority, define its limits, or make itself the owner of
its meaning. Parliament did not create Te Tiriti.
Instead, we will use legislation to bind Crown conduct to obligations arising from Te Tiriti, establish
independent mechanisms to bring the Crown to account, and resource Māori to lead the
constitutional transformation that comes next.
This legislation binds the Crown. It does not bind Te Tiriti.
ENDS THIS LEGISLATION BINDS THE CROWN, NOT TE TIRITI.
```
